quote: We think in words, but our stream of consciousness is steered below the level of words, by the trained-in remnants of past insights and harsh experience
content: Claim: conscious verbal thought is steered by processes operating below the level of words and awareness. This is broadly consistent with dual-process accounts of cognition (Kahneman, 2011, Thinking, Fast and Slow; Evans & Stanovich, 2013, https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691612460685), in which fast intuitive ("System 1") processes feed deliberate reasoning. The existence of fast, non-deliberate influences on judgment is well-supported, and expertise-based intuition is documented (Klein, 1998, on naturalistic decision making). Caveat: strong claims about unconscious determinants of complex behavior should be distinguished from many "automaticity" and social-priming demonstrations of the 2000s, a number of which failed to replicate (see Open Science Collaboration, 2015, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716).

quote: it is how human beings think by default, how they have thought since the ancient times
content: Claim: substituting a vacuous causal node ("skip-over") for genuine understanding is the human default mode of thinking. This relates to the "cognitive miser" framework (Fiske & Taylor, 1991) and to evidence that people accept shallow, fluent explanations without checking them (Cognitive Reflection Test, Frederick, 2005, https://doi.org/10.1257/089533005775196732; illusion of explanatory depth, Rozenblit & Keil, 2002, https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog2605_1). These effects replicate. The universalizing historical claim ("since the ancient times") is rhetorical and not itself an empirical finding.

Claim: terms like "complexity" and "emergence" create an illusion of understanding. This is directly supported by the illusion of explanatory depth (Rozenblit & Keil, 2002, https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog2605_1) and the "seductive allure" effect, in which irrelevant technical or neuroscientific phrasing raises perceived explanatory quality (Weisberg et al., 2008, https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn.2008.20040; replicated and extended by Weisberg et al., 2015, https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500006410). The effect is robust.

Claim: "complexity" never does explanatory work, even though it has rigorous definitions like Kolmogorov and VC complexity — the failure is always the "skip-over," not the word. The anecdote's lesson is sound for hand-waving usage, but it understates how much real predictive content the technical notions carry, which weakens the inference from "this conversation misused the word" to "appealing to complexity is a microthought, not a thought." There are substantive, falsifiable theses of the form "system X cannot perform task Y unless its description length / sample complexity / circuit complexity exceeds a bound": VC dimension yields concrete generalization bounds (Vapnik, 1998), and computational-complexity arguments place hard limits on what bounded agents can compute. Marcello's intuition that "there's got to be some amount of complexity that does it" is, charitably read, a claim about necessary representational capacity — which is a respectable open question in learning theory, not merely a verbal evasion.

Claim: the right discipline is to refuse to "skip over" any mysterious step and instead linger at the gap until it is mechanized. As a research ethic against premature closure this is valuable, but taken as a universal rule it cuts against productive scientific practice, where black-boxing a sub-problem and reasoning around it is often how progress is made. Working physicists routinely posited unexplained primitives (the quantum of action, the cosmological constant, dark matter as a placeholder "missing mass") and built predictive theories on top of them before any mechanism was in hand; thermodynamics succeeded for a century while "entropy" remained a useful black box prior to statistical mechanics. The skill is knowing which gaps must be confronted now versus deferred — a judgment about research strategy and tractability that the blanket "never skip over" injunction does not by itself supply.
